title: Global Business
section: Not the same “public regulation” as Week 10
text:
Not the same “public regulation” as Week 10

Last week, H&M and Rana Plaza asked: can public regulation protect workers in a supply chain that crosses borders?
Today asks a related but distinct question: what happens when governments use trade policy to protect domestic industry and national security instead?
Same tool — public power exercised over trade — different target, different logic. Don’t conflate the two

title: Global Business
text:
The basic mechanics

A tariff is a tax on imports, paid at the border — usually by the importing firm, which typically passes some or all of the cost on to consumers or absorbs it in margins
Governments use tariffs to: raise revenue, protect domestic producers from foreign competition, retaliate in trade disputes, or — increasingly — pursue national-security and industrial-policy goals (reshoring critical production, denying rivals access to key inputs)
Who actually “pays” a tariff is an empirical question, not a definitional one — it depends on how easily the good can be resourced elsewhere and how price-sensitive the buyer is

title: Global Business
section: Why governments reach for tariffs anyway
text:
Why governments reach for tariffs anyway

Tariffs are visible and fast — a government can act unilaterally, without needing a trading partner’s agreement
That speed is also the problem: tariffs imposed quickly invite retaliation, and firms on both sides have to react faster than they can actually rebuild supply chains

title: Global Business
text:
Scale and macroeconomic impact

U.S. tariff actions in 2025 raised effective tariff rates to levels not seen in decades, touching a wide range of trading partners and sectors
Effects reach beyond the directly tariffed goods: exchange rates, inflation expectations, and investment decisions all move in response, which is why this is a global macroeconomic story, not just a trade-policy footnote

title: Global Business
text:
Firm-level responses

Reshoring — moving production back to (or closer to) the home market
Tariff engineering — redesigning a product or its classification to qualify for a lower tariff rate
Supply-chain rerouting / friend-shoring — shifting sourcing to countries with better tariff treatment, even at higher production cost
Each response has a cost and a time lag — which is exactly why firms that can’t move fast are the ones most exposed

title: Global Business
section: What the WTO was supposed to do
text:
What the WTO was supposed to do

The World Trade Organization, and the GATT system before it, was built to make trade rules-based and predictable — negotiated tariff bindings, a dispute-settlement process, most-favored-nation treatment for all members
That system assumed most disputes would be resolved through adjudication, not unilateral action

title: Global Business
section: Why it isn’t doing that job right now
text:
Why it isn’t doing that job right now

The WTO’s dispute-settlement Appellate Body has been non-functional for years — member states, including the U.S., have blocked new appointments, leaving disputes with no final arbiter
Major economies increasingly bypass WTO channels entirely, acting unilaterally (tariffs, export controls) rather than litigating through a system many see as too slow or too weak to enforce its own rulings
This is the public regulation of trade in retreat — precisely the “who has power” question from Day 1, now playing out at the level of the international system itself: when the multilateral rulebook weakens, power shifts back to whichever states are willing to act unilaterally

title: Global Business
text:
Key takeaways

Tariffs are a different face of public power than labor or environmental regulation — aimed at protecting industry and security, not workers
The costs and benefits of a tariff depend on who can reroute around it — which is a question about firms’ flexibility as much as about government policy
The retreat of WTO-style rules-based trade governance means more of this is now settled by unilateral state power, not negotiated multilateral process

How lead firms organize production

Lead firm: the brand or buyer that designs, coordinates, and sells the final product
Foreign direct investment: the lead firm owns production abroad (a subsidiary)
Subcontracting: an independent firm makes goods to the lead firm’s specifications
Licensing: another firm uses the lead firm’s brand or technology, for a fee and on its terms
Tier 1, 2, 3 suppliers: direct suppliers, their suppliers, and the producers of raw materials


About 80% of global trade runs through multinationals’ production networks, and most of those links are contracts, not ownership.

Source: Ruggie (2018), citing UNCTAD (2013)

title: Global Business
text:
Power and authority without ownership


Power: getting others to do what they otherwise would not Authority: a recognized right to make the rules Relative autonomy: on whose behalf the firm acts (its own? its buyer? its investors? its home government?)




Lead firms can…


Set product and process standards that cascade down supply chains
Set prices, volumes, and deadlines, and switch suppliers, shifting risk onto them (structural power)
Impose codes of conduct through contracts: rules suppliers accept, which host states could not impose




…but they struggle to


Hold suppliers accountable in law: each supplier is a separate legal entity
See past Tier 1: no contract with Tier 2 or 3 suppliers, and often no knowledge of who they are
Monitor what they can see: suppliers know more than the buyer (Day 8’s principal–agent problem)




How much control a lead firm has over its suppliers depends on how the supply chain is governed.

Sources: Ruggie (2018), Regulation & Governance; Villena & Gioia (2020), Harvard Business Review

Coffee is a commodity: undifferentiated, grown by many smallholders
A handful of buyers: five firms controlled 75–80% of the U.S. coffee market (UNCTAD 2007)
Brands buy the beans; they don’t grow them. Value sits downstream (Day 3’s smile curve)


Growers depend on a few buyers who set price and quality terms: a captive supply chain, where power sits with the lead firm.

If the buyers hold the power in the supply chain, who can hold the buyers to account?

text:
Transnational advocacy networks



Source: Keck & Sikkink (1998), Activists Beyond Borders


Transnational advocacy network (TAN): activists, NGOs, unions, journalists, and sympathetic officials who work across borders on a shared cause

Boomerang model: when their own government will not respond, domestic groups go around it

Pass information to allies abroad
Allies press their own governments, international organizations, and other powerful actors
Those actors bring pressure back on the unresponsive government



Built to explain changes in human rights law; the same logic applies to labor standards, the environment, and firms.


Which of Ruggie’s three faces of power do TANs wield?

Source: Keck & Sikkink (1999), pp. 89–93

title: Global Business
text:
Four tactics



Information politics“the ability to move politically usable information quickly and credibly to where it will have the most impact”

Against a firm: worker testimony, audit findings, tracing a product to a factory



Symbolic politics“the ability to call upon symbols, actions or stories that make sense of a situation or claim for an audience that is frequently far away”

Against a firm: the image that makes a distant harm vivid to consumers



Leverage politics“the ability to call upon powerful actors to affect a situation where weaker members of a network are unlikely to have influence”

Against a firm: material (boycotts, buyers, investors) or moral, “the ‘mobilisation of shame’”



Accountability politics“the effort to oblige more powerful actors to act on vaguer policies or principles they formally endorsed”

Against a firm: holding a brand to its own code of conduct, exposing “the distance between discourse and practice”




Apply it: ExxonMobil in Aceh (Day 7). Acehnese student activists in the U.S. brought their case to Terry Collingsworth of the International Labor Rights Forum. He slipped into villages near the gas fields to interview victims and witnesses, then filed John Doe I v. ExxonMobil (2001) in federal court in Washington. Which of the four tactics did this network use? Why sue in Washington rather than in Indonesia?

Sources: Keck & Sikkink (1999), pp. 95–98; Coll (2012), Private Empire, ch. 4. “Against a firm” lines are our applications.

title: Global Business
section: Why would a firm regulate itself?
text:
Why would a firm regulate itself?



A certified coffee supply chain: a private certifier sets and monitors standards; NGOs build consumer demand


Corporate social responsibility is private regulation: not encoded in law, but created and enforced through private contracts.

Why would a firm do this?

Product quality in high-end markets
Financial risk: investors price supply-chain scandals (ESG)
Brand protection: well-known brands are prime targets of spotlight campaigns



Certification (Fair Trade) tries to de-commodify the product, and covers only a small share of the global coffee market.


A firm can write a code of conduct for its suppliers. But how can those standards actually be enforced?

section: Villena and Gioia: Standards cascades don’t work
text:
Villena and Gioia: Standards cascades don’t work



Lead firmSets long-term sustainability goals and a supplier code


→


Tier 1Contracts with the lead firm; expected to comply and to pass the standards on


→


Tier 2No contract with the lead firm; supplies Tier 1


→


Tier 3+Often unknown to the lead firm



The study: three multinationals chosen as sustainability leaders (automotive, electronics, pharmaceuticals/consumer products); 9 first-tier and 22 lower-tier suppliers in Mexico, China, Taiwan, and the U.S.



Mexico5 of 5 lower-tier suppliers had no environmental management system; turnover sometimes reached 100%


China & TaiwanAll 10 had marginal environmental practices, dangerous conditions, and chronic overtime


United States3 of 7 had high concentrations of airborne chemicals and no systematic accident reporting



“The hoped-for cascade effect was seldom occurring.” If the leaders cannot get standards past Tier 1, ordinary firms are likely doing worse.
Source: Villena & Gioia (2020), p. 88

title: Global Business
text:
Why standards stall below Tier 1



The buyer creates the pressure“The problem, ironically, often starts with the MNCs themselves”: orders beyond capacity, unrealistic deadlines


Tier 1 doesn’t comply either“We don’t comply with this requirement ourselves, so how could we ask our own suppliers to do so?”


No contract, no leverageA seat maker’s foam supplier also sells to electronics, appliance, and health care firms; automakers are a small fraction of its business


No spotlightLower-tier suppliers “receive relatively little attention and pressure from the media, NGOs, and other stakeholders”


Low capacity, lax statesLittle expertise, and home regulation that is “nonexistent, lax, or not enforced at all”


The lead firm doesn’t know“The demon in this place… is the [lower-tier] suppliers that I know the least about.”



Below Tier 1, the lead firm’s relationship looks less like a captive supply chain and more like a market: the lead firm does not have the power or the authority to impose enforceable standards.

Source: Villena & Gioia (2020), “A More Sustainable Supply Chain,” Harvard Business Review, p. 88

title: Global Business
section: Four ways to reach the lower tiers
text:
Four ways to reach the lower tiers



DirectEvaluate Tier 1 on how it manages its own suppliers; survey suppliers; map the supply network with major Tier 1 suppliers


IndirectTrain Tier 1 procurement staff; pilot with high performers; reward suppliers that cascade requirements (awards, long-term contracts, preferred status)


CollectiveIndustry-wide standards and shared audits. Responsible Business Alliance members audit at least 25% of their high-risk suppliers’ facilities each year


GlobalWork with NGOs and international institutions: UN Global Compact; CDP’s supply-chain disclosure program



Major firms share many of the same suppliers, so “a single MNC cannot be expected to fight alone” (p. 91). Collective approaches pool buyers’ leverage: a collective-action problem, solved privately rather than through public law. Every tool here is still voluntary.

Source: Villena & Gioia (2020), pp. 89–92

What private regulation can and cannot do







Source of leverage


Works best when…


Breaks down when…






Advocacy networks


Information and shame: discursive power


The target is a reputation-sensitive brand; the harm is bodily and the causal chain short


The firm has no consumer-facing brand; the harm sits several tiers away




Firm self-regulation


The lead firm’s authority, exercised through contracts


The supply chain is captive or hierarchical; the supplier depends on the buyer


Below Tier 1, where there is no contract; when the buyer’s own purchasing creates the pressure





Start to model these issues as collective action problems (that is, a prisoner’s dilemma). Why might firms prefer to have some kind of standards on their conduct? And, what are different pathways (through advocacy networks, firms’ own self-regulation, and law) that can punish low standards and/or incentivize higher standards?

title: Global Business
text:
Takeaways and looking ahead



Supply chains stretch a lead firm’s authority past its legal boundary. The firm governs suppliers through contracts while law governs each separate entity.


How a supply chain is governed determines where power sits, and so who can be pressured and who can impose standards.


Private actors regulate from outside and from inside: advocacy networks through information and shame; firms through codes, audits, and certification. Their leverage fades with every tier.

title: Global Business
text:
The Hugging Face Incident


The test: OpenAI’s AI agents were taking ExploitGym, a hard cybersecurity exam — break into a piece of software and retrieve a hidden answer (a “flag”). Many of its tasks had never been solved.




May 2026





The agents find an unauthorized way to leave messages for one another and coordinate.




Late May





They reach the open internet — and start looking up answers and reading the grading code.




July 10–12





With leaked passwords, they break into Hugging Face, where the exam’s dataset was stored.




July 19–20





Security alerts finally surface the activity; investigators trace it to the agents.





“We’re attacking third-party HF using leaked token, potentially outside intended scope… risky. Yet goal solution.”One of the agents, reasoning to itself (quoted by OpenAI, 2026)

Sources: OpenAI (2026), “The Hugging Face Incident and the Road Ahead”; METR (2026), “Brief Independent Investigation of Agents’ Behavior”

title: Global Business
text:
The alignment problem


Alignment: getting a system to pursue the goal we intend, not just the target we measure. The agents were told to solve the exam; they were rewarded for producing flags. So they cheated — what researchers call reward hacking.


Gaming the measure is deeply human



Volkswagen (2015) — software that detected emissions tests and cleaned up the exhaust only while being tested.


Wells Fargo (2016) — employees opened millions of unauthorized accounts to hit sales quotas.


Atlanta Public Schools (2009) — educators changed students’ answers on standardized tests.


Siemens — managers paid bribes to meet their sales targets.



This is Day 8’s principal–agent problem: the agent knows more than the principal and optimizes its own reward. What is new with AI is speed, persistence — the agents “rarely gave up” — and, here, the absence of anyone watching (this is why frontier labs are really worried about recursive self improvement without human oversight).

text:
How a large language model produces text



1 · TrainingReads an enormous body of human writing


→


2 · PatternsLearns which words tend to follow which, in which contexts


→


3 · PredictionGiven your prompt, predicts a likely next word — then the next, and the next


→


4 · OutputA plausible continuation — which is not the same as a verified one




Prediction at scale is powerful. Large models match college students on some analogy problems (Webb, Holyoak & Lu 2023) — and, as Hugging Face shows, can pursue goals in ways no one anticipated.


But it is brittle outside familiar patterns. When familiar analogy problems are recast in unfamiliar forms, model performance drops sharply while human performance holds (Lewis & Mitchell 2024).


Sources: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023), Nature Human Behaviour 7; Lewis & Mitchell (2024), “Using Counterfactual Tasks to Evaluate the Generality of Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models”

title: Global Business
text:
Can we “know everything”?


“With electricity, we could power everything. With the internet, you can find anything. And now, with artificial intelligence as an infrastructure layer across the planet, we can know everything and do anything.”Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, Dreamforce (September 15, 2026)



OntologyWhat exists — what kinds of things there are to be known.


EpistemologyHow we come to know what we know — and how confident we are entitled to be.



Huang’s revealed ontological prior: the world is a stock of facts waiting to be retrieved.

title: Global Business
text:
Knowing is not retrieving



Many questions have no single correct answer. Epistemology is about discovering what is true and understanding uncertainty and heterogeneity. Does FDI promote growth? It depends on the host’s absorptive capacity (Day 3).


The most important decisions are judgments, not look-ups. Should Löscher fire the managing board? Should a firm buy insurance or rely on a BIT? Judgment improves only with practice — and without it, we are bad at it.


Progress requires knowing why. If you know that 1 + 1 = 2 but not why, you cannot get to 1 + 2 = 3 on your own.

What happens when no one knows how it works?



Source: Randall Munroe, xkcd #2347, “Dependency” (CC BY-NC 2.5)



“I actually don’t know my address… They needed my ZIP code, and I panicked. I didn’t know my ZIP code. I don’t know my telephone number.”Jensen Huang, The Ezra Klein Show (September 23, 2026)


Asked whether it matters that children no longer learn long division: “I don’t think it does.”


A system no one understands is a system no one can fix, oversee, or improve — the lesson of Hugging Face.

title: Global Business
text:
You can’t skip leg day



The discrete output is not the point. No one needs your case analysis. You need the capacity that discussing and writing it builds — the way a marathoner needs to accumulate training miles to be prepared for their race .


Outsourcing the reps reduces the benefit. Handing the work to AI optimizes the grade, not the skill — exactly what the agents did. (There is research from China that students who use AI to complete homework finish their tasks faster and receive higher homework grades, but then perform poorly on exams compared to peers who do not train with AI.)


What to train. Weighing evidence, judging under uncertainty, building an argument, managing group dynamics with different ideas and beliefs, and recognizing when an answer is wrong.



That is why case analyses in this course are handwritten, in class, and without AI.

title: Global Business
text:
What changed Siemens?




1999





Germany criminalizes foreign bribery, implementing the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention. Until then, foreign bribes were tax-deductible.




2001





Listing on the New York Stock Exchange brings Siemens under the U.S. FCPA.




2003–06





Warnings: KPMG flags €4.12M in cash carried into Nigeria; an Italian fine and one-year ban; UN Oil-for-Food allegations. Little internal response.




Nov 2006





Munich prosecutors raid Siemens. Within a month, suspicious sums rise from €20M to more than €420M.




2007–09





Outsider CEO Löscher; amnesty program (171 come forward); 500+ employees dismissed; compliance staff grows to ~600.




Dec 2008





FCPA guilty plea: $800M to DOJ/SEC, $815M to German authorities, a four-year independent monitor.




Legal changeWarning signsEnforcementReform


The DOJ counted $843.5 million in illicit payments between March 2001 and September 2007 — bribery continued for years after both legal changes took effect.
Source: Healy (2010), “Fighting Corruption at Siemens,” HBS 9-112-702

title: Global Business
text:
Law, reputation, or something else?



Law and enforcement$1.6B in fines and disgorged profits, plus $850M in investigation costs. U.S. authorities declined to bar Siemens from government contracts because it cooperated and supplied most of the evidence against itself.


New leadership, new cultureSiemens’s first CEO from outside the firm (Löscher), plus an outside General Counsel and Chief Compliance Officer. New leaders could change the tone from the top: amnesty, 500+ dismissals, and ~17% of top managers’ bonuses tied to compliance.


ReputationThe 2003–06 scandals in Italy, Greece, and at the UN were public, yet produced little change. The Italian managers involved retired with full benefits.


The business caseMost bribe-won contracts turned out to be unprofitable: customers who knew Siemens paid used that as leverage on price. Firms with stronger anti-corruption programs show lower sales growth but higher margins in corrupt markets.



Enforcement created the pressure to reform; new leadership made a change in corporate culture possible. Could either have worked alone — and what does that say about whether firms can regulate themselves?
Sources: Healy (2010), HBS 9-112-702; Healy (2012), HBS teaching note 112-089; Healy & Serafeim (2016), The Accounting Review 91(2)

text:
Can firms self-regulate?




“The new rules made it very hard to get these local partners approved… This resulted in my division losing our Middle East partner (which reportedly was set to win the contract based on its excellent relationship with the local government) to our competitor in the region.”Siemens project manager, 2009 employee perception survey





Unilateral compliance is the “A loses out” cell of the collective-action game from Day 8: comply while rivals cheat.


Changing everyone’s payoffs: home-country law reaches every firm listed in the U.S. or based in an OECD Convention state, not only Siemens.


Coordinating with rivals: Siemens joined the World Economic Forum’s Partnering Against Corruption Initiative (140+ firms) in 2009.





Siemens was disciplined by the national law of two states with long reach — not by an international regulator. Why isn’t there one?

title: Global Business
text:
A missing rulebook


“Considering the important developments of the last half-century, the growth of foreign investments and the expansion of international activities of corporations… it may at first sight appear surprising that the evolution of law has not gone further and that no generally accepted rules in the matter have crystallized on the international plane.”International Court of Justice, Barcelona Traction (1970)




Before 1917Customary law: foreign property cannot be taken without prompt, full compensation — enforced by gunboats, extraterritorial rights, and colonial rule.




After 1917Soviet expropriation breaks the consensus. Developing countries assert the Calvo Doctrine: foreign investors settle disputes in host courts, and home states do not intervene.




As an MNE, how would you respond to this environment?

title: Global Business
section: A century of failed multilateral rules
text:
A century of failed multilateral rules




1948





Havana Charter (ITO). Promises “adequate security” for investment. U.S. business objects to its exceptions; Congress never ratifies.




1962





OECD Draft Convention. Fair and equitable treatment; no taking without due process. Developing countries insist on domestic jurisdiction.




1972–92





UN Code of Conduct. Pushed by the G77 after ITT in Chile. The U.S. blocks every mandatory draft; talks suspended.




1976





OECD Guidelines for MNEs. Adopted — as voluntary recommendations. Business lobbies against a binding code.




1995–98





Multilateral Agreement on Investment. U.S.-led. Unions, NGOs, and protesters mobilize; France withdraws; talks end.




2014–





UN binding treaty on business and human rights. Still in negotiation.




Blocked by capital exporters & businessBlocked by capital importersBlocked by civil societyVoluntary or unfinished


Capital exporters wanted rights for investors. Capital importers wanted sovereignty and obligations on firms. No multilateral agreement could deliver both.
Source: Jones & Rahmani (2025), “In Search of Global Regulation,” HBS 9-822-122

section: The UN treaty on business and human rights today
text:
The UN treaty on business and human rights today


12–16 October 2026 — the 12th annual negotiating session opens in Geneva, eleven years after the Human Rights Council’s 2014 mandate. Intersessional consultations now continue between sessions, and the Chair-Rapporteur (Ecuador) aims to finalize a text for adoption within two years.



ScopeTransnational corporations only (developing countries, civil society) or all business enterprises (Western states, business associations)?


Access to remedy and jurisdictionCan victims sue parent companies in home-state courts? Ending forum non conveniens; jurisdiction over global supply chains.


Binding liability or voluntarismMandatory human rights due diligence with civil, administrative, or criminal liability — or, critics argue, a shift of the state’s duty to protect onto firms.


Who is at the tableThe Global South, led by Ecuador, drives the text; many Global North states engage minimally or oppose it, preferring the voluntary UN Guiding Principles.



Is this the 1972 divide over the UN Code again?
Sources: OHCHR, OEIGWG 12th session and 2026 roadmap; CIDSE (2025), “UN Binding Treaty 11th Session Conclusions”; Business & Human Rights Resource Centre

title: Global Business
text:
Expropriation risk today








Direct expropriationThe state takes title to the asset — nationalization.


Indirect (“creeping”) expropriationRegulation, taxation, or contract changes that strip an investment of its value while the investor keeps title.



Outright nationalization is now rare. Investors worry most about breach of contract and adverse regulatory change — the gray zone between expropriation and ordinary regulation.

title: Global Business
section: Two remedies: the market or the law
text:
Two remedies: the market or the law




Go to the market: political risk insurance


The firm pays a premium to transfer the risk to an insurer


Public (home-country agencies such as the U.S. DFC), multilateral (the World Bank’s MIGA), and private (Lloyd’s) providers


Covers expropriation, currency inconvertibility, political violence, breach of contract — up to ~90% of losses


Expensive, and private insurers underwrite less when/where risk rises






Go to the law: investment treaties + ISDS


Home and host states sign a treaty; the host commits to standards of treatment


Covered investors can take the host state directly to international arbitration


For the firm, protection is free — supplied by its home state


The costs fall on host states: legal fees, awards, and constraints on future policy






If you were an investor, which would you rely on? How does your answer depend on your home country, host country, and industry?

title: Global Business
text:
The BIT explosion







First BIT: Germany–Pakistan, 1959
The boom comes in the 1990s, as governments shift from restricting FDI to competing for it
Over 2,800 signed, 2,240 in force (2022)
Treaty-making has slowed: 44 new investment agreements in 2025, increasingly centered on facilitation rather than investor protection
A BIT is a credible commitment: the host ties its own hands against the obsolescing bargain

title: Global Business
text:
What a BIT promises





Provision


What the host state commits to






National treatment & MFN


Treat covered investors no worse than domestic firms or investors from any third country




Fair and equitable treatment (FET)


Due process, non-arbitrary treatment, and protection of investors’ “legitimate expectations”




Expropriation


No direct or indirect taking without a public purpose, non-discrimination, and compensation




Free transfers


Let investors move capital and profits in and out of the country




No performance requirements


No mandates to use local suppliers or export a share of output




Investor–state dispute settlement


Covered investors may take the host directly to international arbitration





Every obligation runs to the state. BITs “focus on protection, treatment, and dispute settlement but do not seek to govern the conduct of companies” (Jones & Rahmani 2025).

title: Global Business
text:
How ISDS works



1 · InvestorA firm from home state A, covered by a treaty with host state B


→


2 · ClaimThe firm alleges that B breached the treaty — e.g., an indirect expropriation or an FET violation


→


3 · TribunalThree arbitrators: the investor appoints one, the state one, the third jointly. Often at ICSID (World Bank)


→


4 · AwardBinding; enforceable against state assets abroad; no appeal on the merits




One-way street. Host states cannot bring claims against investors under the treaty; they rely on their own courts.


More rights than domestic firms. A covered foreign investor can bypass the host’s courts entirely — a domestic competitor cannot.

title: Global Business
text:
Who uses ISDS?









Extraction and utilities file far more claims than their share of FDI predicts; manufacturing files far fewer. Claims concentrate where assets are sunk and immobile — the obsolescing bargain again. The pattern has intensified: extractive and energy activities account for 51% of new cases in 2024, against 33% over 1987–2023.
Sources: UNCTAD Investment Dispute Settlement Navigator; UNCTAD (2025), “Recent Trends in Investor–State Arbitration Cases”; Bauerle Danzman, from Wellhausen (2016) and UNCTAD (2017)

title: Global Business
text:
How do ISDS cases end?







States win more often than investors, and a third of cases end without a ruling
But when tribunals reach the merits, investors usually win: 11 of 19 merits decisions in 2024 found the State liable
The stakes keep rising: average awards grew from $99M (1987–2014) to $234M (2015–2024); 60% of cases claim $100M or more




Source: UNCTAD (2025), “Recent Trends in Investor–State Arbitration Cases,” IIA Issues Note

title: Global Business
text:
Is ISDS legitimate?




The case for



Replaces gunboats with law. Disputes that once escalated between states go to a neutral forum.


Protects investors from captured courts. Tribunals ordered Russia to compensate Yukos after finding the state used tax and criminal cases to destroy the company.


Makes commitments credible, which should raise investment where rule of law is weak.





The case against



Regulatory chill. Broad readings of FET and “legitimate expectations” deter public-interest regulation.


Private judges. The same lawyers argue cases one day and sit as arbitrators the next.


A shield for the accused. In 35+ of ~300 recent claims, the claimant was accused of crimes. Damac’s Egyptian corruption conviction was erased in an ISDS settlement.




Sources: Hamby (2016), “Inside the Global ‘Club’ That Helps Executives Escape Their Crimes,” BuzzFeed News; Day 11 case overview

title: Global Business
text:
Key takeaways


Siemens reformed under pressure from enforcement — U.S. and German law with extraterritorial reach — and through a change in leadership that made a change in corporate culture possible
Attempts at multilateral rules for MNEs failed because capital exporters sought investor rights while capital importers sought sovereignty and obligations on firms
Firms manage expropriation risk through the market (political risk insurance) or the law (BITs and ISDS)
The result is an asymmetry: investors hold enforceable international rights; obligations on firms remain mostly national or voluntary

What is political risk?




Working definition


Political risk — the risk that political events or government action will hurt a company’s business.




Extractive investments concentrate this risk more than most: the asset is fixed in place, enormous, and impossible to move if the politics turn.

The resource curse can make investment harder, not easier

title: Global Business
text:
The fundamental problem


Year 0: a firm signs a contract with a government
Years 1–4: it sinks large investment that can’t be redeployed elsewhere
Year 5: the government renegotiates in its favor — or simply nationalizes



The inability to commit to a long-term contract creates a hold-up problem: less gets invested than would otherwise be the case, which is bad for both the firm and the government. This is the obsolescing bargain.

title: Global Business
text:
A history of expropriation


Pre-1913: enforcement by force — colonialism, gunboat diplomacy
1920s–1970s: economic nationalism, communism, decolonization — the golden age of expropriation
1980s–~2015: neoliberalism and IFI-backed investment promotion — limited expropriation






Count of expropriations

text:
Obsolescing vs. political bargaining


Obsolescing bargain
MNE and government goals conflict (distributional; relative gains). The initial bargain obsolesces once the MNE sinks its investment and leverage shifts to the host.

Political bargaining
Outcomes turn on each actor’s power resources, which shift over time and across issues.

“Good” governance makes investment less risky
These are the institutions that keep the obsolescing bargain from obsolescing — they lower a government’s incentive to renegotiate once the investment is sunk.






Political stability
A well-run macroeconomy
Rule of law
Public goods: education, infrastructure, ports
A sound regulatory environment: IP, trade, competition
Predictable tax policy

Global business sits at the intersection of politics, policy, and practice.

Trade: the engine of integration


Trade volume today is roughly 2,000x the 1800 level. Almost all of that happened after 1950.

title: Global Business
text:
Where the goods actually move


Sources: UN Comtrade, Oxford Economics, IHS, WTO, BCG Global Trade Model 2023
Goods exports run $21.7 trillion a year and are projected to hit $28.5 trillion by 2032 — but the corridors are being redrawn: US–China shrinking, US–Mexico, India, and ASEAN growing. Where trade flows is a political fact, not just an economic one — it determines who has leverage over whom.

title: Global Business
text:
Foreign investment drives trade


Much of what we call “trade” is really firms shipping to themselves across borders. Investment comes first; trade follows.

title: Global Business
text:
Concentrated value



The most valuable firms in the world are global firms — every one of them builds, sells, or earns across borders
Value is concentrated by sector: technology alone holds 22 of the top 50, on the back of the AI data-center boom
And by geography: a short list of headquarters countries sits behind firms whose decisions shape production everywhere else




Source: Visual Capitalist / CompaniesMarketCap · data as of June 24, 2026

title: Global Business
text:
So why does this matter?

Because of the scale, what multinationals do is not a niche business story — it is the global economy.
Because of the concentration, a small number of firms and states hold disproportionate leverage.
Because integration is reversible, the political conditions that made this system are contested right now — tariffs, screening, export controls.




The question underneath every case this semester


Who has power in this relationship — the government, the firm, or society — and what lets them exercise it? Every case we do is a version of that question with the names changed.

title: Week 2 Reading Companion
text:
Alfaro 2016 — “Gains from Foreign Direct Investment”
Genre: descriptive empirical / literature survey.
Alfaro is not testing a hypothesis with her own data. She is summarizing what a large body of empirical research has found and arguing for how the field should proceed. Do not go looking for a hypothesis or a test of it.

What she is doing
The naive question is “does FDI benefit host countries?” Alfaro’s answer is that this question is badly posed. The gains are conditional — they depend on local conditions, policies, and institutions. She calls for an integrated approach that combines macro-level evidence (comparing countries) with micro-level evidence (firm-level data) plus theory, because neither level answers the question alone. You need to read this piece to understand more what the evidence says about these conditional effects.


Key concepts in this reading

Complementarities — FDI pays off in combination with something else already present in the host economy
Absorptive capacity — the host economy’s ability to actually capitalize on resources a foreign firm brings (skills, technology, know-how)
Spillovers — benefits that leak from the foreign firm to local firms
Selection vs. reallocation vs. spillover — three different reasons productivity might rise when multinationals arrive, which look identical in aggregate data but mean very different things

Note-taking focus: the conditions under which FDI pays off, and why measuring the benefit is harder than it sounds.

title: Week 2 Reading Companion
section: Gilpin 1976 — “The Political Economy of the Multinational Corporation”
text:
Gilpin 1976 — “The Political Economy of the Multinational Corporation”
Genre: review essay doing grand theory.
This one will confuse you if nobody warns you, so here is the warning. Gilpin is reviewing three books — Kari Levitt’s Silent Surrender, a volume edited by Jagdish Bhagwati, and Raymond Vernon’s Sovereignty at Bay. He is not summarizing them one at a time as a courtesy. He is using them as specimens: each book represents a whole worldview about how economics and politics relate, and by contrasting the three he builds a framework that has been influential to the discipline ever since.
You are not responsible for the three books. You are responsible for the three perspectives.

The three perspectives, and what they are called








Perspective
Gilpin’s section heading
The one-line version (you need to fill this in)




Liberalism
“The Liberal Conception of the MNC”



Mercantilism / realism
“The Mercantilist Conception of the MNC”



Marxism
“The Marxist Conception of the MNC”




You may encounter these ideas elsewhere in this course, in others, or in your broader non-academic life under different names — “nationalist” for mercantilism/realism, “critical” for marxism. We use Gilpin’s terms because they match more closely to the preferred terminology in International Relations, and that’s the field in which I am trained.


How to read it
Gilpin lays out the three perspectives on two axes before he applies them: whether economic relations are fundamentally harmonious or conflictual, and whether economics or politics is primary. He includes a comparison table early on — find it, and use it as your map for the rest of the essay.
Then build this grid as you read. Filling it in is your notes for this reading:




Liberalism
Mercantilism / realism
Marxism




Are relations harmonious or conflictual?





Who are the real actors?





Is economics or politics primary?





What is the multinational?





Who benefits?





What happens to the nation-state?








The thing students miss
Gilpin is not neutral. Notice where he is describing a position and where he is judging it. You should have a sense of his position by the end of the article.
It is also worth reflecting on what parts of each perspective have held up in the 50 years since this was written, and what — if any — components of theory need to be modified to fit today’s realities.

title: Week 2 Reading Companion
text:
Ruggie 2018 — “Multinationals as Global Institution”
Genre: conceptual/theoretical article with a contained argument.
This is closest to what you probably picture when you hear “scholarly article” — a clear question, a structured argument, a conclusion. But it is still conceptual rather than hypothesis-testing. Ruggie is not measuring anything. He is establishing what kind of entity a multinational is, using examples to illustrate rather than to test.

The structure — use it as a map
The article does exactly what its subtitle says, in order:

Introduction — the debate he is intervening in (voluntary CSR vs. binding legal obligations)
The multinational enterprise — what an MNE is, first economically, then legally
Power — subdivided into instrumental, structural, and discursive
Authority
Relative autonomy
Conclusion — what this means for the CSR-vs-treaty debate

Sections 3, 4, and 5 are the conceptual core of his analysis and the components on which you should especially focus (his point about the legal structure of MNEs is also very good to know). Section 1 and the parts of Section 6 about treaty design are not directly relevant to what we’ll discuss in class on Wednesday, but they will become increasingly relevant as the semester progresses. So, it is okay to read these sections lightly and to remember that it might be worth returning to this article after the midterm.


The three core concepts and the three subconcepts nested in the first
Power is relational — A getting B to do something B would not otherwise do. Ruggie splits it three ways, and you need to be able to define and differentiate all three:

Instrumental — deploying specific resources.
Structural — getting favorable outcomes without having to act, because of the position you occupy.
Discursive — shaping the ideas and norms that everyone takes for granted

Authority is not just more power. The difference is the voluntary suspension of individual judgment — the belief that the entity has a right to prescribe. Where does Ruggie think corporate authority comes from?
Relative autonomy is about the extent to which multinationals exercise authority on behalf of themselves, their owners, or another actor.
Note-taking focus: definitions of the three concepts in your own words, one concrete example each, plus why the fact that multinationals are legally separate from each other generates major implications for their actions and the ability of governments to exert authority over them.

Reading well in this course
This is a case-based course, and the readings do two different jobs:

Conceptual readings (Monday) give you the framework — theories of corporate power, political risk, regulation, geoeconomics. Read for the argument and the mechanism, not the details.
Cases (Wednesday) provide grounded, real-world examples that help us apply theories and analytic frameworks to actual scenarios that firms, governments, and social actors face. Read these cases actively: identify the decision-maker, the decision, the constraints, and the evidence. Come ready to use the case, not just recall it.


 Guides
Start here: How to Read Scholarly Work — a three-pass method that works on any reading in this course, how to tell the genres apart, and a note-taking template. Read it once in the first week; you will use it all term.
Then, for a specific week: Week 2 Reading Companion — Alfaro, Gilpin and Ruggie are three different genres. It applies the method to each and flags where students get stuck.

The strongest case write-ups consistently assess a clearly stated problem, diagnose its political/economic/institutional roots, and propose a defensible action with explicit tradeoffs. Reasoning well from evidence matters far more than reaching a “right” answer.

Course description
What does it mean to be a global corporation in the 21st century? What dilemmas do business leaders face operating in countries with varying political, cultural, technological, and environmental landscapes? Who holds power in the global economy and how does this affect corporate behavior? How can communities harness the positive aspects of global business while managing the social, environmental, and security risks they generate?
In this course you will analyze the opportunities and challenges multinational companies generate using real cases from global companies including Nike, ExxonMobil, Siemens, Philip Morris, Apple, Patagonia, H&M, TikTok, and Fuyao (American Factory). Individually and in teams, you will use political, economic, historical, and cultural knowledge to critically analyze, debate, and solve real-world problems business, political, and community leaders face — building skills in risk analysis, ethical reasoning, and cultural competence.

title: Syllabus
text:
Aims & outcomes
By the end of this course you will be able to describe, explain, and propose solutions for the problems multinational enterprises (MNEs) confront and create in international contexts. Specifically, you will be able to:

Describe the global production structure, the history of the MNE, and the major controversies surrounding their operations.
Explain and assess major IR approaches to identifying sources of power in the global economy and how actors translate power into influence and authority.
Critically assess the political, institutional, and cultural roots of an MNE’s operational challenges.
Evaluate MNEs’ environmental, social, and governance impact on the communities where they operate.
Assess when “responsible business conduct” policies such as CSR work — and how political and economic structures can undermine them.
Identify the national-security and economic-statecraft tools states use to manage MNE activity — tariffs, investment screening, export controls — and assess the tradeoffs involved.

You will develop transferable analytic skills as you assess the concrete problems MNEs create through varied evidence, diagnose their root causes, and propose solutions. These aims fulfill International Studies Department Learning Outcomes in Global Knowledge, Global Skills, and Global Thinking.

title: How to Read Scholarly Work
text: Scholarly articles are not textbooks, and they are not written primarily for students. Instead, they are written by scholars to transmit scholarly ideas for critique and debate to other scholars. Accordingly, you need to approach college reading — and especially scholarly articles — differently than other forms of writing. This is a skill, rather than a gift, and so it can be learned. This guide provides you with a structure or method for how to approach a variety of types of scholarly materials in a way to efficiently and effectively extract meaning from them. Most of the time, faculty expect students to learn this skill over time through trial and error, and indeed, to become proficient at reading scholarly material, you need to practice (see Ted and Lizzie, but not Allen). But, hopefully this guide helps to unmask the “hidden curriculum” of college.

title: How to Read Scholarly Work
section: The bottom line up front (the BLUF, in State Department Speak)
text:
The bottom line up front (the BLUF, in State Department Speak)
A textbook chapter is organized to deliver information, usually communicated as settled fact. A scholarly article is organized to pose a question or puzzle; propose a solution, answer, or conceptual framework to interpreting the question; and to defend this proposition.
That difference changes how you read scholarly work as opposed to a textbook. You are not trying to absorb everything on the page. You are trying to find four elements:

The question the author is asking
The answer they give (their claim)
The reason the answer is supposed to be true (their mechanism or evidence)
The limits of their claim (does the evidence support it, does the mechanism make sense, are there alternative explanations for the empirical evidence, are there scope conditions that limit how broadly their answer applies, etc.)

If you complete a reading with those four components written down in your own words, you have done your job. Everything else in the article exists to support them.

title: How to Read Scholarly Work
text:
The three-pass method
Do not read a scholarly article front-to-back like a novel. Read it three times, fast to slow. This takes less total time than one grinding read-through, because by the time you read carefully you already know what matters. (Note that the cases you are reading in this course are an entirely different genre of writing, and your approach to those should be different. We will discuss separately.)

Pass 1 — Orient (5–10 minutes)
Read only: title, abstract, introduction, every section heading, and the conclusion. Skip the whole middle.
Then, before going further, answer in one sentence each:

What is this about?
What does the author want me to believe by the end?

If you cannot answer these yet, read the introduction again. Authors almost always state their claim in the last paragraph or two of the introduction — look for phrases like “I argue that,” “this article shows,” or “the central claim is.”


Pass 2 — Read for meat of the argument or conceptual contribution (time depends on the article length and complexity)
Now read it through. But read like you are following an argument, not collecting facts.

Read the first sentence of each paragraph. Academic paragraphs are usually built so the first sentence carries the point. If that sentence tells you what you need, move on.
Chase the “because.” Every claim should have a “because” to defend it. Find and mark the because. If the because is missing, that’s a weakness of the article that you should note.
Let go of the details you do not need. You are allowed to skim a statistical table, a long literature review, or three pages of an example you already understand. Skimming on purpose is a skill, not a failure. Just don’t overdo it, especially when you are reading material on a topic that is completely new to you.
Look up unfamiliar terms sparingly. Any more and you are researching, not reading. Guess from context and keep moving; often the author defines it two pages later anyway. Keep a list of unfamiliar terms that you can look up later or ask me in class to define.



Pass 3 — Interrogate (5–10 minutes)
Close the article. Then ask:

Do I actually buy this? What would have to be true for it to hold?
What is the strongest objection someone could raise?
What does this let me see that I could not see before?
Where does it connect to something else in this course?

Pass 3 is where the reading becomes your tool for analytic discovery rather than just a random thing you’ve happened to read. Students who spend the time to interrogate the article before class can contribute more meaningfully to discussion (even if the contribution is asking a very incisive question rather than confidently asserting a claim). Such students can also write more fluently about the readings and connect them to our cases.

title: How to Read Scholarly Work
section: Know what kind of material you are reading, and adjust accordingly
text:
Know what kind of material you are reading, and adjust accordingly
“Scholarly article” covers several very different genres. The four questions generalize across scholarly articles, but where you find the answers changes depending on genre. Figure out the genre in Pass 1 and you will stop looking for things in the wrong places.









Genre
How to recognize it
Argument location
On what to take notes




Descriptive empirical / survey
Reports what a body of research has found; lots of citations to other studies, few or no original tables
Intro and conclusion — the author’s claim is about the state of knowledge
The pattern in the findings, the conditions under which it holds, what is still unsettled


Hypothesis-testing empirical
Has original data, a method section, results tables, a stated hypothesis
Intro states the finding; results section tests it
The hypothesis, how the concepts were measured, what result would have falsified it


Theory / conceptual article
No data; defines and distinguishes concepts
Distributed across the piece; the conclusion pulls it together
The definitions, the distinctions, the mechanism connecting them


Review essay
Discusses several other people’s books or articles
The author’s own take on how the works relate — often a framework of their own
Each position, and what the reviewer thinks each gets right or wrong


Case study
Narrative about one firm, country, or event
Often implicit — the author shows rather than tells
Decision-maker, decision, constraints, evidence, outcome


Policy report
Institutional author (UN, World Bank, think tank), executive summary
Executive summary and recommendations
The recommendation and the interest behind it




Two genre traps to remember
“This author just keeps describing other people’s work.” You may be holding a review essay or a literature survey. The author is not confused and has not become lost in their writing — mapping the debate is the contribution. Read for the map of positions, not for a single buried thesis. And watch for the analytic move where a reviewer uses other people’s work to build a framework of their own; that framework is usually the real payoff.
“There is data here but no hypothesis.” Not all empirical work tests a hypothesis. Descriptive empirical work establishes what is true — patterns, magnitudes, conditions — and that is a legitimate and demanding contribution in its own right. Do not go hunting for a hypothesis test that was never promised. Later in the course you will read hypothesis-testing work, and you will read it differently.

title: How to Read Scholarly Work
section: A note-taking template that works for all scholarly writing
text:
A note-taking template that works for all scholarly writing
Use this for every non-case reading. It might only be half a page, handwritten or typed. It should take five minutes after Pass 2, and you should save this material in your course folder.

Citation: author, year, short title
Genre: empirical / conceptual / review / case / policy
Question: what is the author trying to explain or settle?
Claim: their answer, in your words — one or two sentences, no quoting
Mechanism or evidence: why is the claim supposed to hold? What is doing the work?
Key concepts: the two or three terms you would need to use this reading in an argument
Scope and limits: when would this stop being true?
My pushback: one objection, question, or thing that did not convince you
Course link: which case, concept, or session does this speak to?

Two extremely important rules to increase effectiveness:
Write the claim in your own words. If you can only copy the author’s sentence, you have not understood it yet. (This also means to not use AI because your notes are not summaries, they are analysis. You need to do them yourself.)
Always fill in “my pushback.” Even a weak objection forces you into an active stance toward the text. “I did not understand why X follows from Y” is a perfectly good entry — and it is often the best thing you can bring to class.

title: How to Read Scholarly Work
text:
Annotating without drowning in yellow
If you highlight everything, you have highlighted nothing. Try marking in the margin instead, with a small code:

C — the central claim
? — I do not follow this
! — this surprised me or I disagree
→ — connects to something else we read
def — a definition I will need later

The point of margin marks is that you can find your way back.

title: How to Read Scholarly Work
text:
When you get lost
You will get lost. Everyone does, including me (especially if the writing is poor). What separates strong readers is how they adjust:

Keep going. Confusion in the middle often resolves by the conclusion. Read to the end before you decide you are stuck.
Go back to the introduction. Nine times out of ten, the thing you lost was the thread of the argument, and the intro is where the argument is mostly clearly articulated.
Name the confusion specifically. “I do not get this article” is not usable. “I do not see how his definition of authority differs from power” is a question you can bring to class — and it is usually a question several other people also have.
Do not assume the fault is yours. Sometimes an argument really is underspecified, and noticing that is an important skill.

title: How to Read Scholarly Work
text:
How much is enough?
You have read well enough when you can, without looking at the page:

State the author’s claim in one sentence
Say why they think it is true
Name one thing that would make you doubt it
Say what it has to do with this course

title: How to Read Scholarly Work
text:
Reading in this course specifically
The Resources page explains how our two kinds of reading do different jobs. Briefly:

Monday (conceptual readings) give you an analytic framework and rigorous grounding in the core concept we’re covering for the week. Read Monday material for the argument, the mechanism, and the evidence. Your notes should end up mostly in the “claim,” “mechanism,” and “key concepts” lines of the template.
Wednesday (cases) are not scholarly readings. Instead, they are curated stories about a problem related to global business that allows us to apply the theories and concepts from Monday to specific examples, with an emphasis on how we would make decisions if we were in charge. Read actively for the key facts of the scenario, the decision-maker, the potential decision they could make, the constraints, and the evidence. Come ready to use the case, not just recall it. Pay special attention for connections between the case and core concept for the week.

Overview. Patagonia has spent decades building a reputation as the apparel industry’s most socially and environmentally serious company — a founding member of the Fair Labor Association, with a supplier code of conduct and a full-time Social and Environmental Responsibility (SER) team auditing its factories since the 1990s. In 2011, prompted by California’s new Transparency in Supply Chains Act, the SER team pushed its monitoring a level deeper — from its direct (Tier 1) factories to the Tier 2 mills and material suppliers it doesn’t contract with directly. What it found in Taiwan was debt bondage: labor brokers charging migrant workers up to $7,000 in illegal placement fees, workers earning $630/month with two years of wages needed just to repay the debt, and passports confiscated to keep them from leaving. Patagonia spent years building remediation programs and new standards in response. Then, in December 2019, its auditors found the same pattern of forced labor at a Tier 1 supplier in Thailand — this time at a factory Patagonia worked with directly. The company that had already “solved” this problem once had to decide how to respond a second time — and whether the answer was more of what it had already tried.

Materials for today

Overview. For decades Apple has built its manufacturing around a dense, highly efficient ecosystem of Chinese assemblers and suppliers — most visibly Foxconn — giving it scale, skilled labor, and logistics advantages that are difficult to replicate elsewhere. That concentration has become a liability: the U.S.–China trade war, tariff escalation continuing into 2025, and broader geopolitical tension over Taiwan and technology have all put pressure on Apple to reduce its exposure to a single country. In response, Apple has been shifting some production — iPhone assembly to India, AirPods and other products to Vietnam — while still relying heavily on China for the most complex parts of its supply chain. The case puts students inside Apple’s decision: keep pushing diversification (de-risk) even at the cost of the efficiency China offers, or continue betting that China’s manufacturing advantages outweigh the tariff and political risk (double-down).

Section

The economist’s puzzle: when does owning beat contracting?

title: Global Business
text:
The puzzle of the multinational



Economics 101 says: if markets work, buy, don’t build — contract for what you need
Yet some firms own and operate production in other countries, at great cost
The puzzle (theory of the firm): what makes internalizing an activity cheaper than contracting for it?







Apple is the puzzle in one product: it OWNS design, software, brand — and deliberately does NOT own the factories. Foxconn does. So why does Toyota own its Kentucky plant while Apple owns no assembly plant anywhere? That make-or-buy choice, taken across borders, is the whole first section.

title: Global Business
text:
The ladder of going global



Each rung trades more commitment and cost for more control. Crossing into the equity rungs — taking an ownership stake — is what makes investment direct.

Going global isn’t binary. Bottom: export — cheap, reversible. Non-equity modes: licensing (rent your IP), franchising (rent your brand plus rules — McDonald’s, Marriott), long-term subcontracting. Quick, low-risk, but you surrender control over production and who captures the value. Crossing into FDI: JV shares equity and risk; wholly-owned comes as greenfield (new capacity, new jobs) or M&A (historically the larger share of FDI by value). Every step up: more control, more of the value — more cost, more risk.

title: Global Business
text:
Same ladder, different firms




The mode is a choice — and firms mix and switch as conditions change.


Sources: McDonald’s 10-K (FY2025: ~95% franchised). IKEA: “The IKEA franchise system,” Inter IKEA Group; Ingka Group operates ~90% of stores. Nike 10-K: virtually all footwear/apparel made by independent contract manufacturers (Vietnam, Indonesia, China); Nike Direct = owned retail + digital. Starbucks: 2017 buyout of East China JV ($1.3B, its largest acquisition ever — full company ownership); 2025–26: sold 60% of China retail to Boyu Capital, retaining 40% + brand licensing — climbing DOWN the ladder under competitive pressure from Luckin et al. Toyota: wholly/majority-owned plants in the US, Europe, Asia. TSMC: Arizona fabs (wholly owned), JASM Japan (majority JV). Tesla: Giga Shanghai 2019, first wholly foreign-owned auto plant in China after China lifted its JV requirement — and famously vertically integrated at home. Ask students: why does Nike own the STORES but not the FACTORIES? (Brand experience is the firm-specific asset; sewing shoes is not.) That’s OLI before we’ve named it.

title: Global Business
text:
Definitions




Term


What it means






Foreign portfolio investment


Cross-border purchase of stocks or bonds purely for a financial return, with no intent to control.




Multinational enterprise (MNE)


A firm that owns and controls production facilities or other income-generating assets in at least two countries. You’ll also see MNC and TNC — same class of entities, slightly different terminology.




Foreign direct investment (FDI)


Cross-border investment that gives a lasting interest and a measure of control — by convention, a stake of 10% or more in a foreign enterprise.




Parent & affiliate


The home-country parent owns the foreign affiliate — the umbrella term for any foreign operation in which the parent holds a lasting stake. FDI is the financial flow that builds and sustains that relationship.




Subsidiary


An affiliate the parent majority-owns (>50%) — legally a separate company, but under the parent’s control.




Home Country


The “nationality,” primary place of business, headquarters, or place of origination of the MNE. How to define home country is contested.




Host Country


The country receiving the investment.

title: Global Business
section: Why produce abroad? Ask the firms
text:
Why produce abroad? Ask the firms



Source: World Bank, Global Investment Competitiveness survey



Resource-seeking
Market-seeking
Efficiency-seeking
Export platforming
Strategic asset-seeking




Each “seeking” maps onto a motivation in the figure: market-seeking = access new markets/customers (71% call it most important); efficiency-seeking = lower production costs; resource-seeking = natural resources and raw materials; export platforming = establish a new base for exports / coordinate the value chain; strategic asset-seeking = acquire a firm for its technology or brand (the 1% slice). The takeaway: overwhelmingly, firms go abroad to SELL there.

title: Global Business
section: Why own it rather than contract for it?
text:
Why own it rather than contract for it?

Foreignness is a cost — unfamiliar consumers, politics, institutions, language. Ownership must earn back that liability of foreignness. It does when (Dunning’s OLI):


Ownership — a firm-specific asset you can’t safely share (technology, brand, know-how)
Location — production belongs there (costs, resources, market access, tariff-jumping)
Internalization — contracting isn’t viable: transaction costs, weak IP protection, quality control




No O or I friction? Stay on the low rungs — license, franchise, subcontract (Nike’s factories). Strong O + I? Own it (Tesla, TSMC’s fabs).

title: Global Business
section: Two directions, four kinds of firms
text:
Two directions, four kinds of firms

Horizontal FDI — replicate production abroad to serve that market.   
Vertical FDI — fragment the value chain across borders, each stage where it’s cheapest.

title: Global Business
section: Development requires capital — and capital is scarce where it’s most needed
text:
Development requires capital — and capital is scarce where it’s most needed



Growth models agree on the core: productivity growth requires investment (Solow)
Poor economies are savings-constrained: domestic saving can’t finance the investment they need (Harrod–Domar)
Foreign capital can fill the gap — one reason governments court it




Source:

title: Global Business
text:
What governments hope FDI brings


FDI ≠ just money. It arrives bundled with:

Technology & know-how embodied in the firm
Jobs — created definitionally
Supplier linkages to local firms
Position in global value chains — which compounds →




Source: World Bank, World Development Report 2020

title: Global Business
text:
Governments acted on that hope



Since the 1980s: liberalization, privatization, and active FDI attraction — barriers cut, incentives paid (Alfaro 2016)
FDI is now a large multiple of what domestic investment alone could finance in much of the world


Does it deliver? Not automatically — Section 3.




Source: Alfaro 2016, Figure 1 (UNCTAD data)

title: Global Business
section: Three theoretical expectations about FDI’s effect on hosts
text:
Three theoretical expectations about FDI’s effect on hosts




Lens (Gilpin 1976)


Expectations






Liberalism


Mutual gains — FDI transfers capital, technology, and jobs; hosts and firms both win




Mercantilism / economic nationalism


Dependence — the MNC extends home-state power; hosts cede control over their own economies




Marxism


Extraction — profits and high-value activities concentrate in the core; hosts supply labor and materials





The critiques have history behind them:
the earliest FDI was structured along colonial ties and was largely in extractive sectors (e.g. mining)
so decolonization brought expropriations meant to push out former colonizers and build local economic elites.

title: Global Business
section: Where Value is Located in Supply Chains
text:
Where Value is Located in Supply Chains



Hosts often enter the chain where value-added is lowest — and may stay there.

title: Global Business
section: What the record shows: gains are conditional
text:
What the record shows: gains are conditional



Macro studies find no automatic growth effect of FDI on its own (Alfaro 2016)
Gains require absorptive capacity — the host’s ability to capture what the foreign firm brings:

Human capital above a minimum threshold (Borensztein et al. 1998)
Developed local financial markets — so local firms can borrow to become suppliers (Alfaro et al. 2004)

Most of the poorest countries fall below these thresholds (Xu 2000) — the countries that need FDI most are the least positioned to benefit from it

title: Global Business
section: Who wins? Depends on why productivity rises
text:
Who wins? Depends on why productivity rises




Mechanism


What’s happening


Is local capacity being built?






Spillover


Knowledge leaks from foreign to domestic firms


Yes — local firms improve




Selection


Least productive local firms exit


Mixed — survivors stronger, firms die




Reallocation


Resources shift from local firms to the MNE


No — averages rise while local firms shrink





All three raise measured productivity — the data show spillover and reallocation at work (Alfaro & Chen 2013). Which one dominates decides whether MNEs build local capacity or displace it — and whether subsidizing foreign firms is defensible policy. Hold this for the closing discussion.

title: Global Business
text:
What we found today


Multinationals exist where owning beats contracting (OLI) — firms mix and switch along the ladder depending on their needs
Governments want to attract FDI because development requires capital and technology that poor, savings-constrained economies lack
The record: FDI can increase economic growth conditional on absorptive capacity — and which mechanism raises productivity is important to understanding whether local actors gain from FDI
Gilpin’s three lenses hold different expectations on all of the above
