title: Global Business
text:
Recap: what drives bargaining power?
Two things about a firm’s position key to predicting how much leverage the host government gains once the deal is signed:

how mobile its capital is, and
how much it needs the host’s own market.






Mobile capital(low fixed assets)


Fixed, sunk capital(high fixed assets)


Small / export-platform market


Firm keeps the leverage. Credible exit threat; the host has little unique to offer.


Some erosion. Assets are stuck, but the host market isn’t the prize.


Large, market-seeking host


Some erosion. Mobile, but the firm needs access to a big domestic market.


Host gains the leverage. The classic obsolescing bargain — assets are sunk and the market is worth staying for.



That’s the political bargaining model: whichever side’s power resources are scarcer or erode faster after signing tips the deal in the other’s favor.

title: Global Business
text:
Defining and managing political risk




Classes of political risk



Breaches of contract — including bribery/corruption
Adverse changes in laws, regulations, and policies
Internal instability — violent conflict, crime, and weak court systems
Geopolitical conflict





Rice & Zegart (2018) reduce effective political-risk management to four questions:


1UnderstandHow much risk will the firm tolerate? — its political risk appetite.


2AnalyzeTurn political uncertainty into political risk — something you can assign a probability to.


3MitigateRaise risk-adjusted return: political risk insurance, government & community relationships, CSR.


4RespondReact well when a risk becomes a real operational hit — and capitalize on the crisis.

title: Global Business
text:
Defining corruption

Corruption: the misuse of publicly derived power and authority for private gain
Bribery: money or favors given to influence the acts of a public official — or anyone entrusted with power (meaning, an authority figure)



By scale


Grand corruption — high-level officials manipulate policy, law, or major contracts for large private gain (e.g., a minister steering a concession to whoever pays them)


Petty corruption — low- or mid-level officials extract small, everyday payments to deliver a service they already owe you (e.g., a bribe to speed up a permit)




By predictability


Pervasive corruption — bribery is the norm; everyone knows the going rate


Arbitrary corruption — unpredictable and ad hoc; paying doesn’t guarantee the outcome

title: Global Business
text:
Corruption as a political risk
Rice & Zegart list corruption among their ten types of political risk: “discriminatory taxation and systemic bribery.” It creates exposure in three distinct ways:


Direct costsBribes raise the cost of doing business, and corrupt agreements aren’t enforceable in court.


A relationship problemHow close to the government is too close? A friendly regime can be replaced — leaving your connections, or your complicity, exposed.


Legal riskExtraterritorial law (FCPA, UK Bribery Act, OECD Anti-Bribery Convention) can reach conduct that happened entirely abroad.

title: Global Business
section: Is corruption an adaptive or maladaptive response?
text:
Is corruption an adaptive or maladaptive response?



“Grease the wheels” Corruption is a workaround for a slow, rigid state — bribes are “speed money.” Huntington: the only thing worse than a dishonest bureaucracy is an honest, rigid one.




“Sand in the gears” Corruption piles extra cost, secrecy, and uncertainty on top of weak institutions — it doesn’t fix the underlying problem, it compounds it.




Zhu & Shi (2019) separate two things that are normally tangled together in real-world data: how often officials demand bribes, and whether paying one actually guarantees the service.


Method: A vignette experiment embedded in a firm survey in China. Each executive was randomly assigned one scenario, rated how attractive that business environment was (1–5), and said how they’d invest.






Service deliveredreliably


Service deliveryis uncertain


Officials rarelydemand bribes


V1 — Clean & efficient


V2 — Clean & inefficient


Officials oftendemand bribes


V3 — Predictable corruption


V4 — Arbitrary corruption



Random assignment isolates the effect of bribery and of uncertainty — in observational data the two are almost impossible to pull apart.
Zhu, Boliang, and Weiyi Shi. 2019. “Greasing the Wheels of Commerce? Corruption and Foreign Investment.” The Journal of Politics 81 (4): 1311–1327. https://doi.org/10.1086/704326

title: Global Business
section: What they found: sand in the gears
text:
What they found: sand in the gears



Source: Zhu & Shi (2019), Fig. 1



Source: Zhu & Shi (2019), Fig. 3




Executives always rate corruption worse than a clean government — even a slow, inefficient one
V3 and V4 are rated about the same. Knowing the going rate for a bribe doesn’t make it acceptable
The one exception: fixed-asset-intensive, high-productivity overseas investors are a little more forgiving of predictable corruption — though still worse off than under clean government



Even in China — arguably corruption’s best-case setting for the “grease” story — the evidence favors sand in the gears.

title: Global Business
text:
Measuring corruption
Corruption is hidden by its very nature, so researchers triangulate two approaches:



Perceptions — surveys of experts and executives (e.g., the CPI)
Experience — did you pay a bribe, and did it work? (what Zhu & Shi just measured directly)
Qualitative differences matter too: low-level vs. high-level, pervasive vs. arbitrary




Source: Transparency International, Corruption Perceptions Index 2023




42/100 — the 2025 CPI’s global average, its lowest in over a decade. 122 of 182 countries score below 50, and only 5 score above 80 (down from 12 a decade ago) — “corruption is worsening globally, with even established democracies experiencing rising corruption.” Source: Transparency International, Corruption Perceptions Index 2025

title: Global Business
section: Corruption as a top-down principal-agent problem
text:
Corruption as a top-down principal-agent problem
A principal delegates authority to an agent to act on their behalf. The agent typically knows more about their own actions and local conditions than the principal does — an information asymmetry the agent can exploit.


Principal delegates authority to agentcitizens & officials · shareholders & managers · states & firms







Compliesacts in the principal’s interest




Divertsuses delegated power for private gain — corruption






Detectedlegal exposure and reputational cost; the position itself is put at risk


Undetectedprivate gain persists; the principal’s interests go unmet






Monitoring alone rarely solves this: the same information asymmetry that makes delegation useful is what makes diversion hard to catch. Also, sometimes leaders are happy to engage in corruption or at least willing to look the other way.

title: Global Business
section: Corruption as a bottom-up collective-action problem
text:
Corruption as a bottom-up collective-action problem
Model two firms (or officials) choosing whether to comply or cheat:






Firm B complies


Firm B cheats






Firm A complies


Best for society


A loses out




Firm A cheats


A gets ahead


Nash equilibrium





Everyone would prefer [Comply, Comply] — but absent enforcement, [Cheat, Cheat] is each individual’s best response. Solving corruption requires solving this rational response.



Best response functionThe strategy that maximizes your payoff, given what you expect the other player to do.


Nash equilibriumA pair of strategies where neither player can do better by switching alone. At [Cheat, Cheat], deviating to Comply only makes things worse for you.


Pareto optimalAn outcome where no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off. [Comply, Comply] is Pareto optimal — but it isn’t the equilibrium.



Is is a collective-action problem because society is better off with the pareto optimal outcome, but is likely to get a suboptimal outcome due to individual, uncoordinated incentives.

title: Global Business
section: Solving the collective-action problem: three potential levers
text:
Solving the collective-action problem: three potential levers




Lever


How it works






Host-country institutions


Rule of law, independent courts and anti-corruption agencies, transparent procurement, whistleblower protection — raise the cost and lower the payoff of cheating at home.




Home-country institutions


Extraterritorial law reaches firms wherever they operate — the FCPA (US), UK Bribery Act, OECD Anti-Bribery Convention. A firm’s own government can punish bribery committed abroad.




Social norms


Kubbe, Baez Camargo & Scharbatke-Church (2024): formal rules only bind if they match what people actually expect everyone else to do. Where corruption is the norm, legal reform alone rarely moves behavior.

title: Global Business
section: Social norms of reciprocity and obligation
text:
Social norms of reciprocity and obligation


Source: Kubbe, Baez-Camargo & Scharbatke-Church (2024), Fig. 1

Baez-Camargo et al. (2020) study petty corruption across Rwanda, Tanzania, and Uganda and find two social norms doing most of the work: reciprocity and obligation to the group.


ReciprocityA gift or favor creates an unwritten obligation to reciprocate. A bribe is rarely a one-off — it’s a social investment that builds a relationship, which is exactly why it’s so hard to refuse: Tanzanian health workers who reject bribes report users getting upset, shouting, and calling them unhelpful.


Obligation to the groupFamilies invest in putting a member through medical school, expecting to be provided for later. When the resulting public-sector salary can’t meet those expectations, the official is pressured to extract rents on the family’s behalf — and risks being shunned by kin if they refuse.



The uncomfortable finding: these are pro-social norms — trust, reciprocity, solidarity — not their absence. Rosenbaum et al. (2013) show prosocial norms facilitate, rather than mitigate, petty corruption wherever formal, legal enforcement is weak.

title: Global Business
section: Can you shift norms of corruption?
text:
Can you shift norms of corruption?


Fragile / mixed: a Nigerian campaign combining a film with a free-to-reply text line spiked corruption reports 1.7× overnight — then collapsed within days. The underlying norm never actually shifted.
More promising, still modest: a Mexican campaign informing people how widely corruption was actually condemned cut stated bribery willingness by ~7 points — but its own author calls it one tool among many, not a fix on its own.
Most promising so far: a peer-led pilot in a Dar es Salaam hospital — staff themselves as anti-bribery “champions,” plus signage resetting perceived norms — produced real, significant drops in patients’ felt need to bribe.



Bottom line (Kubbe et al. 2024): reforms that ignore social norms are, at best, short-lived — and can backfire. Can this be applied to strategic management?

title: Global Business
section: What made corruption pervasive at Siemens?
text:
What made corruption pervasive at Siemens?

Weak leadership and an enabling “tone at the top”
Limited compliance enforcement resources
A changing legal environment (FCPA, the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention, German law)
Global reach across many jurisdictions and norms
Intense competitive pressure to win contracts

title: Global Business
text:
Key takeaways

Corruption is the misuse of public power for private gain and represents a political risk for MNEs that need to opperate in environments with weak institutional constraints on such behavior
The evidence favors the view that corruption is maladaptive - sand in the gears, rather than a method of greasing the wheels. Even predictable corruption is rated worse than a clean but slow government
Corruption persists because the individually rational move (Nash equilibrium) isn’t the collectively best one (Pareto optimal) — and no single lever (law at home, law abroad, or norms) reliably closes that gap alone

title: Global Business
text:
Two treaty webs




Bilateral investment treaties





Bilateral tax treaties





Same architecture: bilateral, written by capital exporters, protecting investors from host states — against expropriation (BITs) or double taxation (tax treaties).


The draft UN Code (1986, never adopted) already asked firms not to set internal prices “to shift the tax base.” What happens when the problem is double non-taxation?
Sources: Day 10 (BITs); Arel-Bundock (2017), Fig. 1; Jones & Rahmani (2025), Exhibit 2

title: Global Business
section: The three pillars of international taxation
text:
The three pillars of international taxation



Source: Zucman (2014), Fig. 1

For half a century, foreign profits were ~5% of U.S. corporate profits — the 1920s rules barely mattered. Today they are about one-third.





1920s, League of Nations: four economists are asked how to avoid double taxation.


1 · Source-based taxation. Profit is taxed where it is earned: Brazil taxes “Coffee Rio.”Loophole: make profit appear to be earned where taxes are zero.


2 · Arm’s-length pricing. Affiliates price trades with each other as if they were unrelated firms.Loophole: transfer mispricing — and many internal assets have no market price.


3 · Bilateral, not multilateral. Thousands of treaties; trade has had the GATT since 1947, tax has no equivalent.Loophole: treaty shopping across inconsistent rules.

title: Global Business
section: Where U.S. firms book their foreign profits
text:
Where U.S. firms book their foreign profits






Source: Zucman (2014), Figs. 2–3



55% of U.S. firms’ foreign profits (~$650B, 2013) are booked in six places: the Netherlands, Bermuda, Luxembourg, Ireland, Singapore, Switzerland



Taxes paid there: about 3% (BEA data; Microsoft’s 2014 10-K implies at most 3.1%)




Havens now hold ~18% of all U.S. corporate profits — a tenfold rise since the 1980s

title: Global Business
section: How do you move profit on paper?
text:
How do you move profit on paper?



Treaty shoppingLocate affiliates to exploit inconsistencies across thousands of bilateral treaties.


Transfer mispricing“Coffee Rio” overcharges its U.S. parent so profit appears in Brazil (25%), not the U.S. (35%). U.S. firms export to low-tax affiliates at low prices and import from them at high prices (Clausing 2003).


Intangibles with no market priceWhat were Google’s algorithms worth in 2003, before its IPO? Patents, logos, and code are rarely sold between unrelated firms, so there is no arm’s-length price to check against.


Intragroup loansA low-tax affiliate lends to a high-tax affiliate; interest payments are deducted where taxes are high and booked where they are low.



Almost all of this is tax avoidance (legal), not tax evasion (illegal). It is also costly: General Electric’s tax department employed close to 1,000 people.
Source: Zucman (2014), pp. 124–127

title: Global Business
text:
The Double Irish Dutch Sandwich



     Google Inc.United States · R&DU.S. rate: 35% Google Ireland Ltd.Ireland · sales and staffIrish rate: 12.5% Google Ireland HoldingsIrish firm, “managed” in BermudaBermuda rate: 0% Google B.V.Netherlands · shell, no staffDutch conduit EMEA advertisersEurope, Middle East & Africa revenue 3 IP rightssold cheaply(2003) 1 license sublicense 2 royalties,0% tax(within EU) 4 direct route:20% withholding royalties, 0% 5 U.S. “check the box”: the IRS treats IrelandLtd. and B.V. as branches of Holdings, so U.S.anti-avoidance rules never apply. U.S. tax isdue only if profits come home. 6 





Google earns most of its non-U.S. profit selling advertising in Europe. Follow the money: where does that profit end up being taxed?


1Google Inc. transfers its search and ad technology to Google Ireland Holdings in 2003, months before its IPO, at what turned out to be a low price. Holdings shares R&D costs; all licensing income is booked here.


2Holdings licenses the technology to a Dutch shell, Google B.V., which sublicenses it to Google Ireland Ltd. — to use Dutch tax treaties.


3Ireland Ltd. sells advertising across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa; Google France pays Ireland for the right to use the technology. Profits are now taxable in Ireland at 12.5%.


4Ireland Ltd. pays royalties to the Dutch B.V. Royalties are deductible, so Irish taxable profit nearly vanishes. No withholding tax applies to payments within the EU.


5The B.V. passes the royalties to Holdings. The Netherlands levies no withholding tax — to the Dutch, Holdings is Irish. Paying Bermuda directly would have triggered Irish withholding tax: hence the Dutch “sandwich.”


6U.S. “controlled foreign corporation” rules should tax these royalties at once. One form (IRS 8832) makes Ireland Ltd. and the B.V. disappear for U.S. purposes; U.S. tax (35%) is owed only if profits are repatriated.


Result: “stateless income.” Google’s effective tax rate on foreign profits: 2–8%. In 2017 alone, €19.9 billion passed through the Dutch B.V. to Bermuda.


Sources: Zucman (2014), pp. 124–126; diagram adapted from Arel-Bundock (2017), Fig. 3; Dutch filings via CNBC (2019)

text:
Stateless income





Tax authority


What it sees






United States (IRS)


Ireland Ltd. and the B.V. do not exist; Holdings is an Irish company. No U.S. tax until profits are repatriated.




Ireland


Holdings is Bermudian (“mind and management” in Bermuda), so it is not taxable in Ireland. Ireland Ltd.’s royalties are deductible.




Netherlands


Holdings is Irish, so royalties pass on to it without withholding tax.




France, Germany…


Google sells there, but its profit appears in Ireland.






“Playing tax treaties against each other… Google thus generates stateless income, nowhere taxed in the year it is generated.”Zucman (2014), p. 126



Ireland decided in 2014 to phase out the Double Irish; Google ended it at the close of 2019. The structure was legal throughout.
Sources: Zucman (2014); CNBC, “Google to end ‘Double Irish, Dutch sandwich’ tax scheme” (Dec. 31, 2019)

title: Global Business
text:
Who pays?



Source: Zucman (2014), Fig. 5



1998–2013: the effective tax rate of U.S. firms fell from 30% to 20% — about $200B a year; at least two-thirds of the decline is profit shifting



Worldwide, corporate tax losses are estimated at $500–600B a year (UNU-WIDER)




Winners: shareholders, and equity ownership is highly concentrated
Losers: governments that fund public goods, and those who make up the difference — labor relative to capital, small firms relative to MNEs

title: Global Business
text:
A race to the bottom



Source: OECD, via Reuters


OECD average statutory rate: ~42% → ~21% in four decades. Ireland: 12.5% from 2003.

The puzzle: profit shifting costs governments revenue. Why, then, do governments keep lowering their own rates — and offering individual firms special deals?




Part of the decline in corporate tax rates may be efficient (perhaps corporations were taxed too highly previously), but the decline likely overshoots the optimal tax rate.

title: Global Business
text:
The tax-competition game






Payoffs: (A, B)


B holds its rate (25%)


B cuts its rate (12.5%)






A holds its rate (25%)


(3, 3)Revenue protected; investment stays put


(1, 4)B draws profit and investment away from A




A cuts its rate (12.5%)


(4, 1)A draws profit and investment away from B


(2, 2)No one gains investment; both lose revenue








Players: two governments, A and B, competing for mobile profit and investment.


Strategies: hold the corporate rate, or cut it.


Payoffs: each government’s ranking of outcomes, 4 = best, 1 = worst. A’s payoff is listed first.



Your turn: what should A do? What should B do? Where do they end up?

title: Global Business
text:
Solving the game






Payoffs: (A, B)


B holds


B cuts






A holds


(3, 3)


(1, 4)




A cuts


(4, 1)


(2, 2)








If B holds, A gets 3 by holding and 4 by cutting → cut.


If B cuts, A gets 1 by holding and 2 by cutting → cut. Cutting is A’s dominant strategy: best whatever B does.


B faces the same choice: cutting is dominant for B too.


Nash equilibrium: (Cut, Cut) = (2, 2). Neither government gains by switching alone.


Both prefer (Hold, Hold) = (3, 3). The equilibrium is Pareto-inferior: a prisoner’s dilemma.





Even if A and B promise to hold their rates, each gains by cheating on the promise. Without enforcement, an agreement is cheap talk.

title: Global Business
text:
Getting out of the dilemma



Change the payoffs of cheatingSanction the defector. FATCA (2010) threatened a 30% withholding tax on U.S.-source income; Swiss, Singaporean, and Luxembourg banks agreed to report U.S. accounts.


Let a large state act aloneZucman: the U.S. could reform its corporate tax with “little to no international cooperation” — or, with the EU, impose tariffs on havens that refuse to cooperate.


Bring everyone inA multilateral rule binds all players at once, rather than through thousands of bilateral bargains.


Beware the holdouts“The more havens agree to cooperate, the bigger the incentives for the remaining ones not to do so.” When Switzerland shares data with France, French evaders move to Hong Kong.



Which of these does the OECD’s global minimum tax use?
Source: Zucman (2014), pp. 136, 142–145

title: Global Business
section: From BEPS to a global minimum tax
text:
From BEPS to a global minimum tax




2013–15





BEPS (base erosion and profit shifting) Action Plan. 15 actions, incl. country-by-country reporting and anti-treaty-shopping rules.




2016





Inclusive Framework. Non-OECD countries join as equals; now about 147 members.




Oct 2021





Two-pillar deal (136 jurisdictions). Pillar One: taxing rights for market countries. Pillar Two: a 15% minimum tax.




2024





Pillar Two takes effect in the EU, UK, Japan, Korea, and others. Pillar One stalls.




2025





The U.S. exits (Jan.). After threats of retaliatory taxes, the G7 accepts a “side-by-side” system (June).




Jan 2026





Side-by-side package. U.S.-parented groups exempted from key Pillar Two rules.




CooperationDefectionAccommodation


BEPS fits Zucman’s first class of reform: harmonize the rules, keep source-based taxation and arm’s-length pricing. Pillar Two adds a floor.
Sources: Zucman (2014), p. 134; OECD; Saint-Amans (2026), Bruegel; Conference Board (2026)

title: Global Business
text:
How the minimum tax works



1 · ScopeMultinational groups with revenue of €750M+


→


2 · MeasureThe effective tax rate, country by country: taxes paid ÷ profit booked there


→


3 · Top upIf the rate is below 15%, a top-up tax makes up the difference (minus a carve-out for real payroll and assets)


→


4 · Collect1st: the low-tax country itself2nd: the parent firm’s home country3rd: any other country where the firm operates




Example: a subsidiary in “Lowtaxia” books €100M of profit and pays €5M in tax. Its effective rate is 5%, so the top-up is 10% × €100M = €10M (before the carve-out). If Lowtaxia does not collect it, the parent’s government will; if the parent’s government does not, other governments will.



The firm pays 15% either way. The only question is which government gets the money — so Lowtaxia’s best response is to collect the top-up itself.

title: Global Business
section: The minimum tax changes the payoffs
text:
The minimum tax changes the payoffs






Payoffs: (A, B)


B keeps ≥15%


B cuts below 15%






A keeps ≥15%


(3, 3)


(4, 1)A collects B’s top-up




A cuts below 15%


(1, 4)B collects A’s top-up


(2, 2)








Cutting below 15% no longer attracts profit: the top-up is collected anyway, by someone else.


Solve it: keeping ≥15% is now the dominant strategy for both.


The equilibrium is the cooperative outcome. Enforcement is built in: a government that cheats only hands revenue to others.



But: it is a floor at 15%, not 25%. Above the floor the dilemma remains — and competition can shift from rates to subsidies and credits.

title: Global Business
text:
The minimum tax in practice



It raises moneyFirst year (2024): $90–124B, 2.4–3.4% of global corporate tax revenue — below the $155–192B forecast. Little evidence of lost investment or jobs. 60+ jurisdictions have implemented it.


The U.S. holeFrom 2026, U.S.-headquartered firms are exempt from the 2nd and 3rd collection steps; low-tax countries can still collect the top-up themselves. The U.S. applies its own 14% minimum, averaged across countries. Review by 2029.


New room to competeA new safe harbor protects “substance-based” tax incentives. The OECD’s revised estimate: $91–155B a year. Without the backstop, low-tax states can again court U.S. firms.


A rival forumUN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation: majority voting, led by developing countries. The U.S. walked out (Feb 2025). Next session: Nairobi, Nov 30–Dec 10, 2026; target: end-2027.



Did the United States defect? Is a floor with a hole in it still a floor?
Sources: OECD (July 2026) via Bloomberg Tax; OECD side-by-side package (Jan. 5, 2026); Saint-Amans (2026), Bruegel; Eurodad (2025); Tax Justice Network (Sept. 2026)

title: Global Business
text:
Key takeaways


International tax rests on 1920s rules — source-based taxation, arm’s-length pricing, bilateral treaties — built to prevent double taxation; globalization turned them into channels for double non-taxation
Profit shifting is mostly legal: treaty shopping, transfer pricing, and hybrid structures like the Double Irish Dutch Sandwich generate stateless income
Tax competition is a prisoner’s dilemma: cutting is each government’s dominant strategy, so all end up worse off
The 15% minimum tax changes the payoffs so cheating hands revenue to others — but the U.S. exemption reopens room to compete

text:
Can a lead firm enforce a standard through its supply chain?





Three questions


What a yes requires


H&M and Rana Plaza






1 · Can it identify the supplier?


Knowing who actually makes the product, past Tier 1


Tier 1 suppliers sometimes subcontracted “without the client’s knowledge”; H&M could not be certain its products were never made in Rana Plaza




2 · Does the supplier depend on its orders?


Being a large share of the supplier’s business


Rana Plaza’s five factories subcontracted for many brands (Walmart, The Children’s Place, Mango); H&M switches factories “whenever a cheaper option was available”




3 · Will it stay after a violation?


A long-term relationship worth protecting


Cutting ties protects the brand, not the workers: Patagonia’s termination paradox





The power to exit is different from, and often contrary to the power to enforce. A brand that can switch suppliers easily has structural power over price, but little leverage over how any one factory treats its workers.


If no single brand has that leverage, who can apply pressure, and on whom?

Sources: Ruggie (2018); Villena & Gioia (2020); Hoffman (2023), pp. 8–10

The data: whose orders, which factories?



Source: Distelhorst & Locke (2018), Figure 3: share of purchasing by exporting countries’ labor-rights ratings



A global sourcing agent matches buyers with factories and audits those factories. Its buyers are mostly retailers (79%), mostly headquartered in North America (73%)

Compliance: the audit grade, A to D. A or B counts as compliant (28% of factory-years)
Orders: each factory’s annual order value, reported in 13 ranges


Audits are snapshots and miss a lot, especially freedom of association. But they are what buyers see, so they measure compliance as buyers perceive it.

Compliant factories received 64% more in orders. Does compliance pay, then?

Not so fast. Compliant factories are also bigger, better at delivery and quality, and located in different places. Any of those could attract buyers on its own. This is a selection effect.


A confounder affects both the explanatory factor (compliance) and the outcome (orders), so the simple comparison mixes several effects together.

text:
The better comparison: each factory against itself



Source: Distelhorst & Locke (2018), Figure 4 (top panel), p. 11



Fixed effects: compare each factory with itself before and after its compliance changes
Difference-in-differences: compare the change for factories that move into compliance with the change for those that stay noncompliant


Rules out: anything about a factory that doesn’t change, such as its country, its products, or its owners. Can’t rule out: things that change within a factory at the same time


Becoming compliant: about 4% more in annual orders [1%, 7%], roughly $110,000 a year. Falling out of compliance brings a weaker penalty.

Clothing is the industry targeted by three decades of anti-sweatshop campaigns. Furniture and cookware were not.


The authors’ interpretation: buyers under activist pressure prefer compliant factories to reduce reputational risk. Compliance with parent standards, then, depends also on a effective social pressure campaigns (boomerang model).

section: What the article can’t tell us
text:
What the article can’t tell us





Limit


Why it matters






Higher prices or more orders?


If the 4% is more orders, a factory earning a 2% profit margin gains just 0.08% (2% × 4%). If it is a higher price, its margin rises from 2% to 6.1%




Does it cover the cost of compliance?


The data include no compliance costs, so we can’t tell whether the extra orders outweigh what it costs a factory to comply




One sourcing agent


The factories’ other buyers may not care about compliance, so the 4% may simply be orders moving between buyers




Scope


Western retailers and light manufacturing; not electronics, minerals, or agriculture




Is it enough?


79% of factories were noncompliant in 2012. Paying a living wage could raise unit prices by 2–12%





“Although the net impact of activist campaigns and resulting private regulatory activities may be positive, this model still falls far short of guaranteeing basic rights for the millions of workers employed in global supply chains.” Distelhorst & Locke (2018), p. 15

Source: Distelhorst & Locke (2018), pp. 14–15; Table 1

title: Global Business
text:
Two different questions



Does compliance pay?

An empirical question about firms’ incentives

Reputation: avoiding the next spotlight campaign
A modest reward in orders, mostly where activists have campaigned
Perhaps a “high road” to growth for small exporters (p. 15)




Should MNEs create a standard at all?

A normative question about responsibility

If a standard protects workers’ lives, should compliance depend on whether buyers reward it? Should state regulation compel compliance instead?
Who should bear the cost of these standards: brands, factory owners, consumers, or governments?
Whose standards are these anyway, and who gets to set them? Private corporate interests? Democratically elected governments? Transnational advocacy networks? Capital exporting countries?

Supply chain structure decides how much a lead firm can impose a standard over its supplier. A brand that can easily switch suppliers can walk away, but it can’t make any one factory comply.
The boomerang can target firms as well as states, and it is most effective when the harm is bodily and the causal chain is short
Compliance pays, a little, and mostly where activists have pushed. That means most factories still don’t have huge incentives to comply

What CFIUS is



The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States reviews foreign acquisitions of U.S. businesses for national-security risk
The U.S. keeps an open investment environment — CFIUS is a guardrail, not a wall
As developing economies (read: China) do more outward FDI, developed countries have grown more worried

When can CFIUS act?
CFIUS can intervene only if:

No other law is adequate to address the national-security threat, and
There is credible evidence the foreign investor might take action that threatens to impair U.S. national security

Remedies run from mitigation agreements and conditions up to blocking a deal or ordering divestment.

Critical technology

Sensitive personal data

title: Global Business
text:
From globalization to geoeconomics

The post–Cold War assumption: keep economics and security separate, and let markets liberalize
Today: governments deliberately use economic interdependence as leverage — what Farrell & Newman call weaponized interdependence
Chokepoints in finance, technology, and supply chains become instruments of power

title: Global Business
text:
Instruments of economic statecraft

Tariffs and trade restrictions — the full topic of Day 20
Export controls (e.g., advanced chips, chip-making tools) — a sharper-edged tool than the tariffs and reshoring pressure Apple’s case (Day 21) illustrates
Sanctions and entity lists
Investment screening (CFIUS — last week)
Industrial policy (subsidies, domestic-content rules) — governments building domestic capacity so firms have somewhere to reroute to
Forced-labor import bans (UFLPA)

Many of these target supply-chain chokepoints where one country holds disproportionate control — precisely the concentration Apple is trying to reduce its own exposure to (Day 21).

text:
Both instrument and target

Instrument: governments enlist firms to comply, decouple, or cut off counterparties
Target: firms get export-controlled, sanctioned, screened, or banned
The result for business: rising compliance costs, supply-chain fragmentation, and pressure to “de-risk” or reshore
